approved: Tax Laws Amendment (Disclosure of MRRT Information) Bill 2013

Moved the Tax Laws Amendment (Disclosure of MRRT Information) Bill 2013 on behalf of the member for North Sydney, which would let tax officers disclose aggregate mining tax instalment figures and require the minister to report them to parliament within six sitting days, and traced the mining tax's five iterations since May 2010, during which forecast revenue collapsed from $37 billion to just $3.3 billion over four years.

Supported the disclosure bill, contrasting the coalition's $26 billion cost of repealing the carbon and mining taxes with roughly $150 billion in accumulated deficits over five years, and noted the mining tax, negotiated in June 2010, was forecast to raise $22.5 billion but has collected only around $200 million so far this financial year.

Opposed the disclosure bill, noting the Tax Office withheld MRRT collection figures after the September 2012 quarter on independent Australian Government Solicitor advice that disclosure could identify individual taxpayers, and argued rising demand from over a billion people in India, 300 million in Indonesia and roughly a billion in China would sustain long-term mining tax revenue.

Supported the disclosure bill, tracing how MRRT revenue forecasts fell from $4 billion to $3 billion to $2 billion before actually collecting only $200 million, and calculated that once forgone company tax and administration costs are counted, the government nets only about 25 cents for every dollar raised, against a current five-year forecast of $5.5 billion down from an original $26.5 billion.

Opposed the disclosure bill, citing a June 2012 Minerals Council of Australia report showing petroleum resource rent tax forecasts under the Howard government were sometimes 40 to 100 per cent inaccurate, with annual revenue swinging between $500 million and $2½ billion, and noting Howard-era forecast errors averaged 27 per cent over its last five years, exceeding 40 per cent on three occasions.
